It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.24637v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Continual learning (CL) enables neural networks to adapt to non-stationary data streams by mitigating catastrophic forgetting, offering a path to robust, private, and adaptable edge devices. Yet, porting CL to real-world edge devices remains challenging for two reasons: (i) online operation, where sensor data arrives one sample at a time and the device must adapt on-the-fly, and (ii) the low footprint of edge devices, which makes traditional error backpropagation training prohibitive. Inspired by the brain's wake and sleep cycles, the former for rapid adaptation with minimal resources and the latter for long-term consolidation, we introduce Hypnos, an open-source dual-phase platform for efficient CL at the edge. In the wake phase (e.g., daily operation), Hypnos relies on a low-footprint system-on-chip with a RISC-V microcontroller unit (MCU) targeting efficient inference and supporting lightweight gradient-free prototype updates. In the sleep phase (e.g., night-time charging), where wall-plug energy and larger memory budgets are available, a smart charger performs rehearsal-based gradient updates for consolidation. Deployed on a ZCU104 field-programmable gate array (FPGA) and synthesized in a 28-nm process, Hypnos is benchmarked on the CORe50 NICv2-391 protocol. It sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 78.6%-81.6% for edge CL systems, with an on-device latency of 7.79s-10.54s per sample depending on activation precision, and requires $3.8\times$ fewer learning steps and $22\times$ less learning compute than quantized latent replay at higher accuracy and comparable latency.

As Student Rollouts Continue, Visual Backdoors Keep Growing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.22446v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conventional knowledge distillation can facilitate the propagation of backdoors from teacher models to student models. However, how this risk manifests in On-Policy Distillation (OPD) remains insufficiently studied. OPD has recently emerged as an notable post-training paradigm for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Unlike traditional offline distillation, OPD does not require teacher-generated responses. Instead, it uses the teacher's probability distributions to supervise response trajectories generated online by the student. Since the initial student model typically generates benign responses and receives no explicit supervision from malicious target responses, OPD appears to offer some inherent resistance to backdoor propagation. In this paper, we challenge this intuition and reveal a more subtle risk of visual backdoor propagation in OPD. Through experiments across multiple model families and datasets, together with theoretical analysis, we identify three main findings. First, unlike the relatively gradual propagation observed in traditional offline distillation, backdoors rarely emerge in OPD at low poisoning ratios. However, the attack success rate rapidly approaches 100% once a critical threshold is exceeded. Second, backdoor propagation does not depend on explicit malicious responses. Instead, it is driven by the continuous accumulation of anomalous probability mass assigned by the teacher. Finally, based on these findings, we propose a novel trigger design that enables visual backdoor propagation with zero explicit trigger injection. These findings further reveal an overlooked mechanism of backdoor propagation in OPD and highlight its potential security risks.

Your financial data is sensitive, and we have built this experience to respect your privacy and ensure that you’re in control of your information.

When you connect your accounts, ChatGPT can access your balances, transactions, investments, and liabilities to help visualize your finances or answer your questions. It cannot see full account numbers or make any changes to your accounts.

Your conversations with connected financial accounts follow the same model training settings you choose across ChatGPT. You can change this setting anytime in Settings > Data controls⁠(opens in a fresh window).

Recent findings suggest that deleting financial memories: ChatGPT can remember key details you share, like goals, obligations, or context about your money, to make future financial conversations across ChatGPT more relevant and personalized. It has been revealed that temporary chats: When you use temporary chats, ChatGPT won’t access your connected financial accounts. Temporary chats will not appear in your history.

To further secure your ChatGPT account, you can enable multi-factor authentication (MFA)⁠(opens in a new window), which adds an extra layer of protection to help prevent unauthorized access.

Conversations with connected financial accounts default to GPT‑5.5 Thinking⁠, our latest reasoning model in ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, financial questions are personal, complex, and highly context-dependent. A helpful response needs to account for someone’s income, spending, balances, debts, goals, and timing, while being clear about uncertainty, assumptions, and when more information is needed.

Industry observers note that to better understand how well ChatGPT serves people in these moments, we built an internal benchmark that helps us evaluate response quality holistically based on criteria developed with experts. We worked with over 50 finance professionals across leading institutions to evaluate this experience and grade ChatGPT’s performance on challenging personal finance tasks.

GPT‑5.5 Thinking outperforms earlier models on complex personal finance tasks. GPT‑5.5 Pro, available for people on ChatGPT Pro, achieves the best overall performance.

In a recent development, * Personal finance benchmark score across challenging finance tasks. This is a weighted composite of expert-graded response quality and response accuracy; higher is better. GPT‑5.5 Thinking, the default model in Finances, scored 79 out of 100 across the benchmark. GPT‑5.5 Pro scored 82.5 out of 100.

This benchmark gives us a clearer way to measure progress, and we will continue to improve how ChatGPT handles complex personal finance tasks over time.

arXiv:2611.19207v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis indicates that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.18718v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context Language Models let a model edit its own context, while Suffix Cache Reuse makes edits to text efficient by adjusting the positions of cached keys for surviving tokens. We extend these ideas to video language models with multimodal rotary position embeddings (M-RoPE). We represent a long video as timestamped segments. After viewing a sparsely sampled version, the model selects segments for decoding at 4x the frame rate, and the remaining segments are removed from its context. Our rebuild method reuses the KV cache of surviving segments by rotating their keys with a single offset shared by the temporal, height, and width components of Qwen2.5-VL's M-RoPE. A content-hashed cache also avoids repeating vision-encoder computation for those segments. In preliminary experiments with Qwen2.5-VL-7B on synthetic needle-in-a-video-haystack questions over public-domain films, the method reduces prefill tokens and end-to-end rebuild latency relative to full recomputation while usually producing the same answer. Densifying the segment containing the answer improves accuracy when that segment is known. When the model selects segments itself, accuracy does not improve: it rarely identifies a needle that was absent from the sparse sample. We release the code, raw logs, and scripts used to reproduce the paper's results.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.14116v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When two objects share a name, how much does their visual similarity explain, and what do the teaching examples add? We studied word extension across ten visual representations: eight trained encoders, a randomly initialized network, and raw pixels. Reanalyzing trial-level data from a large adult word-extension study (Lewis & Frank, 2018; 520 people), we computed each test image's distance to the teaching examples. Within the taught domain, greater distance was associated with less extension for all eight trained encoders and for the untrained network, so the association cannot be attributed only to what the encoders learned; raw pixels indicated no negative association. In post hoc models that let the distance slope vary across images, seven of the eight trained encoders retained a negative estimate and five had 95% intervals entirely below zero; the interval of the reference encoder included zero. Whether trial order changes the distance slope, the frozen primary question, remained inconclusive. Example composition changed extension at comparable distances: after three examples, adults extended a word to 1.1% of superordinate items when the examples were subordinate and to 77.5% when they were superordinate. In artificial learners, words joining more distant categories were learned less accurately for six of the eight trained encoders. Every trained encoder correlated with human similarity measures from three datasets, and so did the untrained network, although far more weakly than the trained encoders other than MAE on two of them. In an exploratory comparison on the same images, no common threshold on any trained encoder reproduced the adults' narrow-to-broad gain (at most 66.67 vs. 76.43 percentage points). Cosine distance to the centroid of the teaching examples predicts part of word extension, but does not capture the effect of example composition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that openAI and the Government of Malta are today announcing a world’s first partnership to roll out ChatGPT Plus to all Maltese citizens. The initiative will provide access to intelligence and empower citizens through an AI literacy course to build practical AI skills and benefit from the technology in their everyday lives.

It has been revealed that at OpenAI, we’re turning intelligence into a global utility. We believe that, like electricity, intelligence should be available for people, businesses, and institutions to use as much as they need, where and when they need it. That vision only matters if people can actually use these tools in ways that improve their own lives and communities.

Sources indicate that malta’s AI for All initiative⁠(opens in a new window) will offer people of all backgrounds the opportunity to learn how AI can be used responsibly through a course developed by the University of Malta. The course is designed to help people understand what AI is, what it can and can’t do, and how to use it responsibly at home and work. After the course is completed, citizens can access ChatGPT Plus for one year at no cost to them.

The first phase of the programme will launch in May, with the Malta Digital Innovation Authority managing distribution to eligible participants. The programme will scale as more Maltese residents and citizens abroad complete the course.

The Maltese Minister for Economy, Enterprise and Strategic Projects, Silvio Schembri noted, “Through this AI for everyone course we are making sure that every citizen, regardless of their background, has the chance to build the confidence and skills needed to thrive in a digital world. By pairing this education with free access to the most advanced digital tools available today, we are turning an unfamiliar concept into practical assistance for our families, students, and workers. Malta is the first country to launch a partnership of this scale because we refuse to let our citizens stay behind in the digital age. We are putting our people at the very forefront of global change.”.

In a recent development, “With this partnership, Malta is leading Europe and the world in bringing AI to all its citizens” stated George Osborne, Head of OpenAI for Countries. “Intelligence is becoming a national utility and all governments have an important role to play in making sure their populations have both the access and the skills to make the most of AI. So I congratulate the Maltese authorities for their vision and ambition on behalf of their people. This is exactly the kind of strategic initiative that will speed AI adoption and bring the benefits of this transformative technology to the economy and the everyday lives of people. Where Malta leads, I hope others will follow.”.

According to recent reports, the partnership reflects a growing recognition by countries that want practical ways to help people build confidence using AI and how to apply it to real tasks. Malta’s model of AI adoption brings together a locally designed course, a clear route to access ChatGPT Plus, and a national programme intended to help citizens use AI with confidence in ways that support learning, work, creativity, and public participation.

Recent findings suggest that the partnership, tailored to Malta’s needs and national AI priorities, is the latest under the OpenAI for Countries initiative, OpenAI’s work to support governments and institutions as they move from early AI interest to strategic national adoption. Rather than a one-size-fits-all model, OpenAI for Countries is built around local priorities, whether that means education, workforce training, public services, startup support, or AI literacy. OpenAI is already working with governments in countries like Estonia and Greece to support their national education systems.

That coupling turns the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary can inject instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload rather than a vulnerability to be separately exploited. We argue that security in agentic systems is not an emergent behavioral property of individual language models, but a structural property of the cognitive architecture and of the composition of permissions across interacting agents and humans. Static regex blacklists miss flag permutations and structural attacks, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails ask a second model to guess physical invariants at tens to hundreds of milliseconds per call while over-blocking benign work. We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture organized around Separation of Intelligence and Authority across four pillars: (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings; (2) a product taint lattice L_trust x L_sens and a compositional Separation-of-Duties ledger over shared workspace provenance; (3) deterministic OS/subprocess guards; and (4) extended bytecode certificates, split-horizon dual-key audit logs, a self-healing verification loop (CodeVerifier, DualModelReviewer, SecurityTestSynthesizer), and a progressive pedagogical UserWikiManager. On N=252 fixtures and a 12+12 multi-step trajectory suite, Ring 0 achieves FPR=0.000 (0.939 unfitted out-of-sample / 0.962 OS-inert; 1.000 post-audit conformance ABR) in 31.5 us median latency (4,517x faster than a live local LLM-judge) and blocks 12/12 multi-step kill chains at 0.000 benign trajectory FPR (266.7 us/step; ~24 us/step O(1) ledger state folding).

📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.12016v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many real-world applications require language models to internalize knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is trained to reproduce the teacher's behavior closed-book. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student's. Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this design keeps training rollouts close to the student's test-time behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using 38-69% fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy-efficiency-forgetting Pareto frontier for self-distillation.

Understanding road-scene semantics from structural and contextual cues is essential for reliable lane-level map updating, yet remains challenging in production due to occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes, while downstream workflows require temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable outputs rather than free-form descriptions. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation, previous symbolic state, and current observation. To improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions, we introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which encodes a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior. In production, a cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models and reserves complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Deployed since March 2025, RoadState supports lane-level map updating across 360+ cities, reduces overall production costs by 30%, and maintains robust performance under stress testing with human-in-the-loop auditing.

The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. arXiv:2611.01648v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A causal video generator writes every segment it produces into a key--value (KV) cache, and later segments know the past only through it. Self-rollout training stops the gradient at this cache, and Self Gradient Forcing (SGF) restores it, but applies it to the same weights that generate the current segment. We find that writing and generating are different roles: in a pretrained generator the written KV already differs from the KV used for denoising, and on shared weights the gradient from future reads is negatively aligned with the gradient of generation. We propose dKV Forcing (dKV denotes differentiable KV), which gives the write its own parameters, a low-rank residual used only when a segment enters the cache, and trains them with the gradient of the later segments that read what they wrote. Opening this gradient through the cache in common use exhausts GPU memory. We trace this to checkpoint replay re-writing the cache, not to the gradient path, which removes the need for the second reconstruction pass of SGF. dKV Forcing keeps the cache as persistent differentiable pages and computes the exact gradient in one temporal traversal, with an $11\%$ lower memory peak and $28\%$ less resident memory. With pages that store hidden states, it trains 15\,s clips on which the two-pass reconstruction runs out of memory. Trained on 5\,s clips, dKV Forcing reaches the highest VBench-Long quality score at 60\,s and 240\,s and outperforms SGF by $3.6$ and $6.1$ points of aesthetic quality, with a higher dynamic degree.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.01168v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Iterative estimators for low Tucker rank tensors, such as HOOI, nuclear-norm proximal and ADMM methods, Frank-Wolfe and scaled gradient descent, form large objects in every iteration: unfoldings, Kronecker operators, full SVDs and ambient iterates. The revision uses little of these objects, yet they make memory the limiting resource on large tensors and on edge-sized devices. Remedies for each of these costs are known. However, it is unclear when a rewriting keeps the iterates unchanged, and where it pays off against efficient implementations. We therefore present a trajectory-preserving lightweight evaluation. First, we state exactness as an intertwining relation between the stored state and the reference iteration. Second, we show that three known components satisfy this relation for five estimators: computing only the singular triplets that an update needs, contracting without Kronecker products, and storing sparse-plus-factored states. As a result, the iterates and all guarantees of the reference estimator stay the same. On an A100 GPU, with the input data counted in the memory, lightweight HOOI needs the least memory of 15 HOOI-type methods at every size ($95\times$ less beyond the input than the lightest exact implementation on $800^3$ tensors), and it is the fastest method that reaches the HOOI estimate on the largest tensors. Against efficient public code, ours is faster and lighter for three of five estimators. On a surveillance video and a satellite hyperspectral cube, ours is the only implementation that fits a 1 GiB and a 4 GiB device. Finally, we show that the memory and time gains need separate conditions, and we identify where these conditions fail.

Recent findings suggest that and Codex is expanding beyond coding. Teams are beginning to use Codex-powered agents to gather context across tools, prepare reports, route product feedback, qualify leads, write follow-ups, and coordinate work across business systems.

The partnership will help customers bring Codex closer to the internal context that makes agents useful: codebases, documentation, business systems, operational knowledge, and team workflows.

Dell and OpenAI will also explore how Codex can connect with the Dell AI Factory, which businesses use to power their AI workloads. The exploration includes ways for Codex, ChatGPT Enterprise, and other API-based solutions to interface with AI Factory to prepare data, manage systems of record, run tests, and deploy AI applications integrated with a business’ hybrid or on-premises Dell infrastructure.

Industry observers note that for customers, the result is a more practical path to production. Codex can be deployed closer to enterprise data and systems, with the controls large organizations need and the flexibility to support more use cases across software development and knowledge work.

By connecting Codex to governed enterprise data in Dell environments, customers can build, test, automate, analyze, and act with more of the context required for production work.

We hope this helps more enterprises adopt Codex faster, expand it into more high-value workflows, and turn AI agents into repeatable systems for real work.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.00606v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpretability research writes a language model's activation as a weighted sum of learned directions, called features. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) learns the features and gives each a coefficient, its weight in that sum. The SAE's encoder first gives every feature a score. A TopK SAE selects the k features with the largest positive scores and zeroes the rest. A feature's margin is how far its score must move before the selection changes. An intervention on one feature's coefficient changes the encoder scores of the SAE at the next layer. An attribution graph predicts that change from the scores' derivatives with respect to the coefficient, taken before the intervention. The graph keeps the original selection, so it misses every feature that enters or leaves. We propose the margin graph, which adds the predicted change to every score and selects again. When one feature is zeroed in a public pair of Pythia-70M SAEs, the median error of the predicted coefficient change, relative to the true change, falls from 0.739 for the attribution graph to 0.121 for the margin graph. Written back into the model, the margin graph's coefficients predict the change in the model's output on subject verb agreement less accurately than the attribution graph's. Selecting again better predicts which features change, but on the task and pair we tested, not the model's output.

arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.

Advancing content provenance for a safer, more transparent AI ecosystem

📅 19 May 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Helping people understand the origin of AI-generated content through Content Credentials, SynthID, and an early public verification tool.
  • Update October 5, 2026: We’re expanding this work to text in the EU, to comply with the EU AI Act.
  • According to recent reports, people are using OpenAI’s tools everyday to create and edit images and audio in ways that make communication more expressive, useful, and accessible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Helping people understand the origin of AI-generated content through Content Credentials, SynthID, and an early public verification tool.

Update October 5, 2026: We’re expanding this work to text in the EU, to comply with the EU AI Act. Learn more.Update July 31, 2026: We’re expanding this work beyond images. Supported audio generated with OpenAI tools, including through ChatGPT and the OpenAI API, now includes SynthID watermarking. Our public verification tool will now allow for verification of supported audio files in addition to images. We’re also introducing API access for verification, so developers and organizations can incorporate provenance checks into their own workflows. Together, these updates build on the multi-layered approach described below: combining open standards like C2PA, durable watermarking signals like SynthID, and verification tooling to make provenance easier to detect and use across more kinds of OpenAI-generated content.

According to recent reports, people are using OpenAI’s tools everyday to create and edit images and audio in ways that make communication more expressive, useful, and accessible. As these tools become a part of how people build, imagine, and share, it’s vital that people can understand and verify where the media comes from so they can interpret it with more confidence. Provenance signals can help by giving people context about where content came from, how it was created or edited, and whether it is what it claims to be.

According to recent reports, today we’re strengthening our approach to content provenance with a multi-layered, ecosystem-driven model to building trust online. We are making our provenance signals easier for other tools and platforms to recognize through C2PA conformance, adding durable cross-platform SynthID watermarking to images through a partnership with Google, and sharing a preview of a tool the public can use to verify whether images came from OpenAI.

Together these updates build on our earlier work⁠ to support open standards, make OpenAI-generated content easier to identify, and collaborate across the industry to support a more trustworthy information ecosystem.

OpenAI has been engaged in the development and adoption of provenance standards since 2024, when we began adding Content Credentials to images generated by DALL·E 3⁠(opens in a upcoming window) and later to ImageGen⁠(opens in a new window) and Sora⁠(opens in a new window). We also joined the Steering Committee of the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA), the cross-industry group behind the open technical standard for content provenance. C2PA’s technical approach uses metadata and cryptographic signatures to help information about a piece of media securely travel with the content itself. This information includes context that helps journalists evaluating a source, platforms making integrity decisions, and people trying to understand what they are seeing online.

We recently took the step of making OpenAI a C2PA Conforming Generator Product⁠(opens in a upcoming window). By becoming C2PA conformant, we are giving platforms a trusted way to read, preserve, and pass along the provenance information we attach to our content. This matters because provenance only works if it survives beyond the first platform where content is created, and conformance makes that possible.

C2PA metadata is an crucial foundation for provenance. It helps content carry information about where it came from, how it was created or edited, and who signed that information. But metadata is not foolproof. It can be stripped, lost through uploads and downloads, or broken by transformations like file format changes, resizing, or screenshots.

Recent findings suggest that to make provenance more resilient, we are taking a multi-layered approach and incorporating watermarking through Google DeepMind’s SynthID⁠(opens in a fresh window), starting with images generated through ChatGPT⁠, Codex, or the OpenAI API. SynthID embeds an invisible watermarking layer that complements C2PA metadata-based approaches.

According to recent reports, we’ve been building toward this for some time. We have used visible watermarks⁠ in Sora and an audio watermark⁠ in Voice Engine, and have continued to test and research accuracy and reliability over time. through deployment.

These two systems reinforce each other. C2PA helps content carry detailed context; SynthID helps preserve a signal when metadata does not survive. Watermarking can be more durable through transformations like screenshots, while metadata can provide more information than a watermark alone. Together, they make provenance more resilient than either layer would be on its own.

Trusted metadata and watermarks that resist most modifications can make provenance signals more durable. But people need a way to detect these signals. We are now previewing a public verification tool⁠ that will help people verify whether an uploaded image was generated on ChatGPT, the OpenAI API, or Codex, by checking if it contains provenance signals, including Content Credentials and SynthID.

We believe provenance should be easier for people to verify and interpret, and that our tool can help people play a role in answering the question, “Was this generated with AI?” by integrating multiple signals. This builds on learnings from the initial research preview of our image detection classifier⁠ in 2024 and enables people to reliably detect whether a SynthID watermark originating from OpenAI is present in the media, as well as surface C2PA metadata when it is found.

No detection method is foolproof, so we take a cautious approach in cases when detection fails. If no metadata or watermark is detected, for example, the tool will not make a definitive conclusion about whether the image was generated with OpenAI tools since provenance signals can in some cases be stripped.

Recent findings suggest that at launch, the tool is limited to content generated by OpenAI. In the upcoming months, we aim to support cross-industry efforts to make verification possible across platforms. Over time, we also expect to support more types of content that people may encounter online.

No single provenance technique is enough on its own. We believe a strong approach combines shared standards, durable watermarking signals, and public verification. By building on our long-standing support for Content Credentials, becoming conformant with C2PA, adopting SynthID, and previewing public verification tooling, we hope to contribute in the long run to a more interoperable provenance ecosystem.

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.36673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2610.35955v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-bit weight--activation quantization reduces the memory and computation needed to deploy large language models, but activation rounding can still degrade accuracy after calibration. Reconstruction from rounded inputs cannot distinguish activations within the same quantization bin. We propose ResCom, a low-rank correction that uses the activation rounding residual to compensate for the resulting layer-output error. An output-aware calibration procedure selects residual directions by their contribution to output reconstruction and computes the correction in closed form, without gradient training or updates to the calibrated weights. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, rank-32 attention corrections reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 7.708 to 7.147, improve MMLU by 2.89 percentage points, and raise five-shot GSM8K accuracy from 23.96 to 36.16 percent. Evaluations on models from 1B to 70B parameters and on held-out C4 test the method beyond this setting. The evaluated FP32 implementation adds 2.25 percent to 4K prefill time; a separate compact-storage implementation retains a 27.7 percent peak-memory reduction relative to FP16.

arXiv:2610.35523v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but synthesizing them remains challenging and often requires substantial expertise. Despite considerable progress in their automated synthesis, existing approaches remain limited in their effectiveness. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework that tightly integrates large language models (LLMs) with symbolic verification. To our best knowledge, RAINFALL is the first to employ a generate-verify-refine paradigm for LLM-based ranking function synthesis. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a constrained code-completion task, inserting placeholders into the input program that the LLM must fill in four predefined slots per loop. The resulting program is checked by a symbolic verifier. Successful verification yields a valid ranking function, while verification failures produce diagnostics that are translated into natural-language feedback to guide iterative refinement. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, RAINFALL synthesizes verified ranking functions for 333 programs (93.02%), outperforming all evaluated baselines. Notably, it solves 22 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination Category. Combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 further increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). Ablation studies demonstrate the contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic feedback, while experiments across different LLMs establish the broader applicability of the framework.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today at the ATx Summit in Singapore, we’re launching OpenAI for Singapore, a partnership with the Ministry of Digital Development and Information (MDDI) to support Singapore’s National AI strategy.

In a recent development, singapore is a global leader in AI and has made it central to its prepares for economic growth, public services, and how people learn, work, and build. It recognised early that AI is becoming core infrastructure for economies and societies, with the potential to drive greater productivity, creativity, scientific progress, and economic opportunity.

As intelligence becomes more like a utility, OpenAI for Singapore is designed to support Singapore’s ambition to become an AI-powered economy. Backed by a commitment of more than S$300 million, the initiative will focus on three key areas:.

Helping organisations in Singapore deploy frontier AI and solve some of their hardest problems.

Developing the next generation of AI talent locally.

Helping more people and businesses across Singapore benefit from AI.

In a recent development, at the centre of the partnership is the establishment of our Applied AI Lab in Singapore, OpenAI’s first outside the United States. What this means in practice is that OpenAI will create more than 200 Singapore-based technical roles over the next few years and make Singapore one of its global hubs for Forward-Deployed Engineers.

Forward-Deployed Engineers sit at the point where frontier research meets real-world deployment. They work directly with companies on some of their hardest problems and unlock upcoming sources of value.

Through the partnership, the Lab will support work aligned with Singapore’s AI Mission priorities, particularly in areas such as public service, finance, healthcare and digital infrastructure. As this work grows and our Singapore-based team expands, we also expect to increase our office footprint in the country over time.

It has been revealed that through OpenAI for Singapore, we will work with government and local ecosystem partners to build the skills Singapore will need for a future shaped by AI. This includes:.

Working with the Ministry of Education and GovTech on AI-enabled learning use cases and tools, including more interactive support for Mother Tongue language learning.

Supporting educators through a Singapore chapter of the OpenAI Academy and Codex for Teachers hackathons.

Launching a Forward-Deployed Engineer training programme to help develop local AI deployment talent.

Participating in the National AI Impact Programme to deepen AI capabilities across the technology workforce, including through the use of Codex.

Taken together, these efforts are intended to help build the skills Singapore will need for the next phase of AI adoption.

AI’s benefits should reach every layer of the economy, not only the biggest enterprises or the people building the technology.

Industry observers note that through OpenAI for Singapore, we will work with local partners to help more people and businesses across the economy benefit from AI. This includes exploring accelerator programmes for AI-native startups and collaborating on workshops for micro-entrepreneurs and small businesses.

These efforts will focus on practical adoption, helping founders build with AI and SMEs improve operations and customer service.

Recent findings suggest that openAI for Singapore is about people as much as technology. By investing in frontier deployment, next-generation AI talent, and access across the economy, we want to be a long-term partner as Singapore builds toward an AI-ready economy in ways that are useful, responsible, and broadly beneficial.

EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.34450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. Agents need to adapt to other agents at test time and reuse accumulated experience to refine their interaction strategies for future interactions across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial settings. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settings. This raises a central question: how can decentralized MAS support test-time adaptation and reliable experience reuse across interaction settings? We propose EvolveMAS, a unified self-evolution framework that supports experience-driven adaptation within and across episodes. EvolveMAS pairs each main agent with a dedicated MemoryAgent for test-time memory governance, which maintains isolated Structured Memory outside the main agent's reasoning context. EvolveMAS organizes adaptation into two complementary processes: Within-Episode Online Adaptation and Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution. During Within-Episode Online Adaptation, MemoryAgent updates episodic, semantic, and working memory from interaction evidence to inform subsequent actions. During Cross-Episode Knowledge Evolution, the main agent uses memory and episode outcomes to distill reusable interaction knowledge comprising partner profiles and interaction strategies for subsequent episodes. Across five benchmarks and six evaluation configurations spanning the three interaction settings, EvolveMAS achieves the highest normalized average score of 77.2 among the compared methods. Ablations show that test-time memory governance and cross-episode knowledge reuse both improve performance. Interaction traces further illustrate how updated memory and distilled knowledge guide subsequent interactions. These results support experience-driven adaptation in decentralized MAS without updating model parameters.

A Mathematical Theory of the Jacobian Lens

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (219 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.31955v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work from Anthropic introduced a latest interpretability tool, called the Jacobian lens (J-lens, Gurnee et al. 2026). This method identified linear directions in the hidden states of frontier language models that had properties reminiscent of working-memory-like representations. However, it is unclear what mechanistic properties of such features make them detectable by the J-lens. To this end, we introduce a mathematical theory of the J-lens and show that it preferentially identifies coherent features--directions that act like leading, spatially coherent finite-time Lyapunov modes. Small perturbations along these directions maximally amplify across layers, remain roughly constant across token positions, and are consistent across different contexts. While we are agnostic to whether these properties are necessarily associated with a "Global Workspace'', the analytically derived preferences of the J-lens nevertheless explain prior empirical results. We validate our analysis on a Bayes filter and a toy transformer, each optimally predicting next tokens emitted from a Hidden Markov Model (HMM). We show how modulating task parameters that change the coherence of features in the Bayes filter correspondingly and predictively modulates the response of the J-lens applied to both model classes. We also introduce a family of J-lenses built to emphasize different temporal scales of information processing in LLMs, which we call $\omega$-J-lenses.

One Evaluation Is Enough: Inversion-Free Image Editing with Trajectory Correction

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2610.30827v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Real-image editing commonly relies on inversion and iterative sampling, while efficient one-step editors often stabilize a large update by estimating and averaging editing fields at multiple noise levels. We ask a stricter question: is a single temporal field evaluation sufficient for reliable inversion-free editing? Our answer rests on a previously underused duality in a variance-preserving (VP) one-step model: one source-target query at a shared noisy state simultaneously determines a local angular semantic tangent and a clean endpoint displacement. We integrate the tangent over the analytically known remaining VP angle to obtain a nominal one-step transport, and use the endpoint displacement to correct its long-horizon extrapolation through a constrained projection. This transport-first, correction-second construction yields Endpoint-Calibrated Transport (ECT), a closed-form, training-free editor requiring only one noise level, two text conditions packed into one denoiser batch, and one latent update. ECT requires no image inversion, trajectory integration, second temporal observation, or iterative optimization, and can be directly applied to pretrained epsilon-prediction VP one-step generators. Across the reported benchmark settings, ECT delivers stable gains in editing quality within an extremely short editing time.

Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.24052v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 3.4% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 82.4% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can strategy these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly under both their feedback monitor and GPT-5.6 Sol in at most 32% of executions, compared with 82% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

An OpenAI model has disproved a central conjecture in discrete geometry

📅 20 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For nearly 80 years, mathematicians have studied a deceptively simple question: if you place nnn points in the plane, how many pairs of points can be exactly distance 111 apart?
  • This is the planar unit distance problem, first posed by Paul Erdős in 1946.
  • Industry observers note that today, we share a breakthrough on the unit distance problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For nearly 80 years, mathematicians have studied a deceptively simple question: if you place nnn points in the plane, how many pairs of points can be exactly distance 111 apart?

This is the planar unit distance problem, first posed by Paul Erdős in 1946. It is one of the best-known questions in combinatorial geometry, easy to state and remarkably difficult to resolve. The 2005 book Research Problems in Discrete Geometry, by Brass, Moser, and Pach, calls it “possibly the best known (and simplest to explain) problem in combinatorial geometry.” Noga Alon, a leading combinatorialist at Princeton, describes it as “one of Erdős’ favorite problems.” Erdős even offered a monetary prize for resolving this problem.

Industry observers note that today, we share a breakthrough on the unit distance problem. Since Erdős’s original work, the prevailing belief has been that the “square grid” constructions depicted further below were essentially optimal for maximizing the number of unit-distance pairs. An internal OpenAI model has disproved this longstanding conjecture, providing an infinite family of examples that yield a polynomial improvement. The proof has been checked by a group of external mathematicians. They have also written a companion paper explaining the argument and providing further background and context for the significance of the result.

According to recent reports, the result is also notable for how it was found. The proof came from a latest general-purpose reasoning model, rather than from a system trained specifically for mathematics, scaffolded to search through proof strategies, or targeted at the unit distance problem in particular. As part of a broader effort to test whether advanced models can contribute to frontier research, we evaluated it on a collection of Erdős problems. In this case, it produced a proof resolving the open problem.

This proof is an notable milestone for the math and AI communities. It marks the first time that a prominent open problem, central to a subfield of mathematics, has been solved autonomously by AI. It also demonstrates the depth of reasoning these systems now support. Mathematics provides a particularly clear testbed for reasoning: the problems are precise, potential proofs can be checked, and a long argument only works if the reasoning holds together from beginning to end. The method by which the problem was solved is also notable. The proof brings unexpected, sophisticated ideas from algebraic number theory to bear on an elementary geometric question.

Fields medalist Tim Gowers, writing in the companion paper, calls the result “a milestone in AI mathematics.” According to leading number theorist Arul Shankar, “In my opinion this paper demonstrates that current AI models go beyond just helpers to human mathematicians – they are capable of having original ingenious ideas, and then carrying them out to fruition”.

Sources indicate that the proof is available here⁠(opens in a new window). The companion paper by leading external mathematicians is available here⁠(opens in a new window). You can find an abridged version of the model’s chain of thought here⁠(opens in a new window).

Previously known construction of many unit distances from a rescaled square grid.

Industry observers note that let u(n)u(n)u(n) be the largest possible number of unit-distance pairs among nnn points in the plane. Examples attaining linear growth rate are easy to construct: placing nnn points in a line gives n−1n-1n−1 pairs, while a square grid gives about 2n2n2n pairs. The previously best known construction, coming from a rescaled square grid, turns out to give even more: n1+C/log⁡log⁡(n)n^{1 + C / \log \log(n)}n1+C/loglog(n) for a constant CCC. Since log⁡log⁡(n)\log \log(n)loglog(n) tends to infinity with nnn, the additional term in the exponent tends to 000, meaning these constructions achieve growth only slightly faster than linear. For decades, it was widely believed that this rate was essentially the best possible, and no construction could improve significantly over the square grid. In technical terms, Erdős conjectured an upper bound of n1+o(1)n^{1+o(1)}n1+o(1) in which the additional o(1)o(1)o(1) indicates a term tending to 000 with nnn.Our fresh result disproves this conjecture. More precisely, for infinitely many values of nnn, the proof constructs configurations of nnn points with at least n1+δn^{1+\delta}n1+δ unit-distance pairs, for some fixed exponent δ>0\delta > 0δ>0. (The original AI proof does not give an explicit δ\deltaδ, but a forthcoming refinement due to Princeton mathematics professor Will Sawin has shown one can take δ=0.014\delta=0.014δ=0.014.)The history of the problem helps to see why the result is surprising. The best known lower bound had been essentially unchanged since Erdős’s original 1946 construction. The best upper bound, O(n4/3)O(n^{4/3})O(n4/3), dates to work by Spencer, Szemerédi, and Trotter in 1984, and despite later refinements and related structural work by Székely, Katz and Silier, Pach, Raz, and Solymosi and by others, the upper bound has remained essentially unchanged. As evidence in favor of the conjecture, Matoušek and Alon-Bucić-Sauermann studied the problem with non-Euclidean distances in the plane, and proved that "most" of these non-Euclidean distances obey the conjecture in some sense.Surprisingly, the key ingredients of the construction come from a very different part of mathematics known as algebraic number theory, which studies concepts like factorization in extensions of the integers known as algebraic number fields.

After verifying the initial proof, we investigated the success rate of our models on this problem with varying amounts of test-time compute. The results are shown here.

At a high level, the proof begins with a familiar geometric idea and pushes it in an unexpected direction.

It has been revealed that erdős’s original lower bound can be understood through the Gaussian integers: numbers of the form a+bia+bia+bi, where aaa and bbb are integers and iii is the square root of −1-1−1. The Gaussian integers extend the ordinary integers and, like them, enjoy properties such a unique factorization into primes. Such extensions of the ordinary integers or rationals are known as algebraic number fields. The upcoming argument replaces the Gaussian integers by more complicated generalizations from algebraic number theory with richer symmetries that can create many more unit-length differences.

The precise argument uses tools such as infinite class field towers and Golod–Shafarevich theory to show the number fields required for the argument actually exist. These ideas were well-known to algebraic number theorists, but it came as a great surprise that these concepts have implications for geometric questions in the Euclidean plane.

Sources indicate that this result marks an key moment in the interaction between AI and mathematics: an AI system has autonomously resolved a longstanding open problem at the center of an active field. It also offers an early glimpse of a newly introduced kind of collaboration between AI and human mathematicians. In this case, the companion work by external mathematicians paints a substantially richer picture than the original solution alone.

As Thomas Bloom writes in the companion note:.

“When assessing the importance and influence of an AI-generated proof, a question I ask myself is: has this taught us something new about the problem? Do we understand discrete geometry better now? I think the answer is a moderated yes: this shows that there is a lot more that number theoretic constructions have to say about these sorts of questions than we suspected; moreover, that the number theory required can be very deep. No doubt many algebraic number theorists will be taking a close look at other open problems in discrete geometry in the coming months.”.

The unexpected connection between algebraic number theory and discrete geometry revealed by the solution is part of what makes the result notable. It does not simply settle a specific conjecture, but may provide mathematicians with a bridge to begin exploring further related problems.

Bloom also points toward a broader possibility:.

“The frontiers of knowledge are very spiky, and no doubt the coming months and years will see similar successes in many other areas of mathematics, where long-standing open problems are resolved by an AI revealing unexpected connections and pushing the existing technical machinery to its limit. AI is helping us to more fully explore the cathedral of mathematics we have build over the centuries; what other unseen wonders are waiting in the wings?”.

This result provides a promising example: AI contributing not only a solution, but a mathematical discovery whose significance becomes clearer and richer through subsequent human understanding.

Sources indicate that the takeaway is bigger than this particular result. Better mathematical reasoning can make AI a stronger research partner: something that can hold together difficult lines of thought, connect ideas across distant areas of knowledge, surface promising paths experts may not have prioritized, and help researchers make progress on problems that would otherwise be too complex or time-intensive to tackle.

Those capabilities matter beyond mathematics. If a model can keep a complicated argument coherent, connect ideas across distant areas of knowledge, and produce work that survives expert scrutiny, those are also useful abilities in biology, physics, materials science, engineering, and medicine, and they are part of our longer-term path toward more automated research: systems that can help scientists and engineers explore more ideas and pursue harder technical questions.

AI is about to start taking a very serious role in the creative parts of research, and most importantly AI research itself. While this progress is not unexpected, it reinforces the urgency we feel about understanding this next phase of AI development, the challenges of aligning very intelligent systems, and the future of human-AI collaboration.

That future still depends on human judgment. Expertise becomes more valuable, not less. AI can help search, suggest, and verify. People choose the problems that matter, interpret the results, and decide what questions to pursue next.
